Welcome toHeat Flow in Sound

In a sound wave, how much heat passes from compression to rarefaction each period?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: two times of a sound wave in air — the wave time 1/ω and the conduction time 1/Dk²

Source

Concept
A log–log plot of two times against the wavelength λ of a sound wave in air at 293 K: 1/ω, in which the phase of the wave changes by one radian, and 1/Dk², in which conduction evens out a temperature variation of wave number k = 2π/λ, D being the thermal diffusivity of the air. Θ(t) is the amplitude of the held copy's T − T₀. Each wavelength visited leaves a blue and an orange dot; open circles mark the current setting; a grey band marks λ < 2πλf, where the air is not treated as a continuous fluid and nothing is plotted or held.
Serves
Relating the heat exchanged between the compressions and rarefactions of a sound wave within one period to the wavelength and to the pressure of the gas.
Inquiry
Five questions read from the screen: the fraction 1 − Θ/Θ(0) conducted from a copy of the gas held still for one period at three wavelengths, the pattern of dots over a sweep of the wavelength, and the dots at 1 mm at two pressures; a closing card sums up. Controls: wavelength λ (0.1 μm to 10 m), pressure p₀ (0.001 atm to 1 atm), and Hold a copy still, which freezes a copy of the temperature profile in the inset and lets conduction alone act on it, its amplitude falling as e^(−Dk²t).
Misconception
Addressed through the answer choices; each choice's feedback points back to a reading of the plot or of the fraction readout.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honours it
Real values, honestly labelledAir at T₀ = 293 K with exact SI constants; c, v̄, λf and D from one model function; the inset's time-lapse is printed on the canvas ("one period shown in 3 s" at 1×, scaled with the shell speed). D is the kinetic-theory estimate; the measured diffusivity of air, 2.1 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s, is about twice it, which changes no conclusion but not every number.
Stable axesλ from 0.1 μm to 10 m and time from 10⁻¹⁰ s to 10⁶ s are fixed; nothing rescales as the controls move.
The student builds the evidenceDots appear only at wavelengths the slider passes through; no line or slope is drawn, so any trend is found by the student.
Model limits visibleThe band λ < 2πλf is shaded and captioned, its edge moving with p₀; the inset greys out and the Hold button is inert there.
Operational measurementThe held copy is drawn with amplitude Θ(0)e^(−Dk²t); the readout 1 − Θ/Θ(0) updates as it fades and is fixed at the one-period value.
Honest drawingThe travelling wave is drawn at steady amplitude, and a note in the Readouts panel says it is drawn without its damping.
Heat Flow in a Sound Wave
Wave time and conduction time against wavelength

Guided Inquiry

1 · Audible sound at 1 atm

Set the pressure to 1 atm and the wavelength to 1 m, a pitch of 343 Hz, and press the button to hold a copy of the gas still. What fraction of the temperature variation of the held copy is conducted away while the wave moves on by one wavelength?

2 · A ten times longer wave

Lengthen the wavelength to 10 m, which lowers the pitch to 34.3 Hz and makes each period ten times as long, and hold a copy still again. How does the fraction conducted away in one period compare with its value at 1 m?

3 · Far above hearing

Shorten the wavelength to 1 μm, where the frequency of 343 MHz is far above the range of hearing, and hold a copy still. What happens to the held copy during one period?

4 · Where the two times meet

Starting from 10 m, move the wavelength slowly down to 0.1 μm, so that the main plot marks both times at every step. Where do the two sets of points meet?

5 · Lowering the pressure

Set the pressure to 1 atm and the wavelength to 1 mm, and note the two points. Then lower the pressure to 0.01 atm. What happens to the points at this wavelength?

6 · Summary

Heat does flow from each compression to the next rarefaction, but across half a wavelength it needs a time 1/Dk² that grows as λ², while the period grows only as λ.

For audible sound in air the fraction exchanged per period is about 10⁻⁴ or less, so the compressions are adiabatic, as Laplace said, not isothermal, as Newton supposed. Conduction catches up only when the wavelength shrinks to a few mean free paths, and lowering the pressure moves that point to longer waves.

Heat Flow in a Sound Wave

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A sound wave heats the air where it compresses and cools it where it thins. Does that heat have time to flow before the wave moves on? This sim sets two clocks side by side, one for the wave and one for conduction, over wavelengths from 0.1 μm to 10 m.

What you'll learn

  • Why Newton's and Laplace's speeds of sound differ.
  • Which two times decide whether heat flow matters.
  • How those times depend on the wavelength and the pressure.
The sim's plot, drawn empty: axes, grey band, inset and legend.

What's on screen

  • Plot: two times in seconds, on log axes, against wavelength. Blue is the wave time 1/ω; the orange is the conduction time 1/Dk2. A point is drawn at each wavelength the slider passes through.
  • Grey band: wavelengths too short for air to be a continuous fluid. Nothing is plotted there.
  • Inset: the excess temperature T − T0 along a sound wave, with arrows for heat flow. Hold a copy still adds a dashed curve for a copy of the gas kept still.
  • Readouts: the frequency, the two times, the mean free path λf, and what a held copy conducts away.
See itSlide the Wavelength control or press the button to jump to 1 mm. Watch for: a point for each time appearing at 1 mm, with its value in the Readouts and the mean free path beside them.

Fixed: air at 293 K with molar mass 28.97 g mol−1, Cp/CV = 7/5, so c = 343 m s−1, and a molecular diameter of 0.37 nm. The diffusivity is the kinetic-theory estimate D = 1⁄3 v̄λf = 1.0 × 10−5 m2 s−1 at 1 atm.

03

Newton's and Laplace's speeds differ in what happens to the heat

Newton, in 1687, supposed that the gas stays at one temperature as the wave compresses and expands it. Then the pressure is proportional to the density, the isothermal bulk modulus is p0, and his speed is (6.14):

Notes (6.14): Newton, isothermal.

Laplace, in 1816, supposed that the compressions follow one another too quickly for heat to flow, so that a compressed gas also grows hotter. Then Pρ−Cp/CV is constant, the bulk modulus is (Cp/CV) p0, and (6.16):

Notes (6.16): Laplace, adiabatic.
Notes, Fig. 88: the adiabat is steeper than the isotherm by Cp/CV.

For a diatomic gas such as air, Cp/CV = 7/5. Which assumption fits depends on one thing: whether heat can flow from compression to rarefaction within a period. The sim compares the two times that decide it.

See itPress Play at 1 m and watch the inset. Watch for: the temperature pattern in the inset moving along, with arrows for the heat flow between its crests and troughs.
04

Heat decays on its own clock, set by the wavelength

A compression is hotter than the gas around it, so heat flows from each compression to the rarefactions half a wavelength away (notes, Fig. 89). Hold a copy of the gas still with T = T0 + Θ(t) cos kx, the same wavenumber k = 2π/λ as the sound. The diffusion equation gives (6.17):

Notes (6.17). D is the thermal diffusivity.
A held pattern decays in a time of order 1/Dk2.

The sound has its own time, 1/ω = 1/ck, in which its phase changes by one radian. The compressions are adiabatic if the decay rate is small beside ω (6.18):

Notes (6.18): small compared with one means adiabatic.

For a gas, D ≈ 1⁄3 v̄mλf, with v̄m the mean molecular speed and λf the mean free path. The sim uses this estimate; the measured diffusivity of air is about twice it, which changes the numbers by a factor of order one.

See itJump to 1 cm and read the two times in the Readouts. Watch for: the wave time 1/ω and the conduction time 1/Dk², each with its own unit.
05

Audible sound barely conducts heat in one period

At λ = 1 m and 1 atm the sound is 343 Hz. The wave time is 1/ω = 4.6 × 10−4 s, and the conduction time is 1/Dk2 = 2.5 × 103 s, about 40 minutes: 5.4 million times longer. A copy held for one period conducts away a fraction 1.2 × 10−6 of its temperature variation.

At 1 m and 1 atm the two times are 6.7 decades apart.

The notes show why, in order of magnitude (6.19):

Notes (6.19). Here λf = 0.066 μm, v̄m/c = 1.35.

So Dk2/ω = 1.9 × 10−7, close to λf/λ = 6.6 × 10−8. The compressions are adiabatic, as Laplace supposed. Newton's formula gives 290 m s−1 for this air, short by about a sixth; (6.16) gives 343 m s−1, larger by √(7/5) = 1.18. Over audible wavelengths, about 2 cm to 17 m, 1/Dk2 is roughly 105 to 108 times 1/ω.

See itHold a copy still at 1 m and 1 atm. Watch for: the conducted-away readout creeping up to 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ as the period ends, with the inset curve staying put.
06

Longer waves are more adiabatic, because conduction time grows as the square of the wavelength

Make the wave ten times longer: λ = 10 m, 34 Hz. The wave time rises tenfold, to 4.6 × 10−3 s. The conduction time rises a hundredfold, to 2.5 × 105 s, about three days. The fraction conducted away in one period falls from 1.2 × 10−6 to 1.2 × 10−7.

At 1 atm, from the grey band's edge to 10 m.

One might expect a slow oscillation to give heat more time to flow, so that low-pitched sound is nearly isothermal. The period does grow in proportion to λ. But 1/Dk2 = λ2/(4π2D) grows as λ2, because a pattern of wavenumber k decays at the rate Dk2. Longer waves are further from isothermal (notes, §6.1).

See itHold a copy still at 10 m and 1 atm. Watch for: the conducted-away fraction ending at 1.2 × 10⁻⁷, a tenth of its value at 1 m.
07

Very short waves conduct a good deal, until the fluid picture ends

Go the other way and the conduction time shrinks faster than the period. At λ = 1 μm and 1 atm (343 MHz) the wave time is 4.6 × 10−10 s and the conduction time is 2.5 × 10−9 s, only 5.4 times longer. It is shorter than the period λ/c = 2.9 × 10−9 s, and a held copy conducts away 0.69 of its variation in one period.

One held copy, one period, at two wavelengths (1 atm).

The grey band begins at λ = 2πλf = 0.41 μm, where kλf = 1. Inside it air is not a continuous fluid, so nothing is plotted or held. The shortest wavelength outside it on the slider is 0.50 μm, where 1/Dk2 is still 2.7 times 1/ω. The two lines approach as λ falls, but in this model they would meet at 2πD/c = 0.19 μm, inside the band.

See itHold a copy still at 1 μm and 1 atm. Watch for: the conducted-away readout rising to 0.69 within the one period, with the dashed inset curve shrinking visibly.
08

Thin air conducts faster, and the fluid picture ends at longer waves

The pressure enters only through the mean free path, λf = 1/(√2 πd2n) with n = p0/kBT0. A hundredth of the pressure gives a hundred times the mean free path and so a hundred times the diffusivity. The wave time is unchanged, since c does not depend on pressure.

At 0.01 atm the conduction line drops a hundredfold (1 atm: faint). Dotted lines meet at the grey dot.

At 1 mm, 1/Dk2 falls from 2.5 × 10−3 s at 1 atm to 2.5 × 10−5 s at 0.01 atm, against a wave time of 4.6 × 10−7 s. The mean free path is then 6.6 μm, and a held copy conducts away 0.11 in one period, against 1.2 × 10−3 at 1 atm. The grey band widens to 41 μm.

Where it matters. The notes point out that c depends on T, Mm and Cp/CV but not on pressure, so measuring c in a gas of known molar mass and temperature gives Cp/CV.

See itHold a copy still at 1 mm and 0.01 atm. Watch for: 1/Dk² reading 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ s, and the conducted-away readout ending near 0.11.
09

Summary

In one line. The sim compares the wave time 1/ω with the conduction time 1/Dk2 to decide whether the compressions of a sound wave are isothermal or adiabatic.

Key points

  • The compressions are adiabatic when Dk2/ω is small, of order λf/λ.
  • 1/ω grows as λ; 1/Dk2 grows as λ2 and is proportional to p0.
  • The fluid picture ends near λ = 2πλf.

Common mix-ups

  • “Slow, low-pitched sound has more time for heat to flow, so it is isothermal.” At 10 m the fraction conducted away is 1.2 × 10−7, a tenth of that at 1 m.
  • “Thinner air is more adiabatic.” At 0.01 atm, 1/Dk2 at 1 mm falls a hundredfold.
  • “The two times cross, so the sim should show where.” They would cross at 0.19 μm at 1 atm, inside the grey band.

Things to try on your own

  • Slide λ from 10 m down to 1 μm and watch the orange point fall faster than the blue.
  • Set 0.50 μm and read the two times either side of the band.
  • Hold a copy at 1 mm for 1 atm, then 0.1 atm, then 0.01 atm.
